fanoutqa_038897.t: Great Britain at the Olympics :: Hosted games :: chunk_0003
fanoutqa_038897.x:
Great Britain at the Olympics :: Hosted games :: chunk_0003
The United Kingdom has hosted the Summer Games on three occasions – 1908, 1948 and 2012, all in London – second only to the United States. At the [2016 Summer Olympics](/wiki/2016_Summer_Olympics "2016 Summer Olympics") in Rio, [Great Britain](/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "Great Britain at the 2016 Summer Olympics") became the first team to win more medals at a Summer Olympics immediately after hosting a Summer Olympics; they won 67 medals overall, coming in second place in the medal table ahead of [China](/wiki/China_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "China at the 2016 Summer Olympics"), two more than in [London in 2012](/wiki/2012_Summer_Olympics "2012 Summer Olympics"). This success came 20 years after finishing 36th in the medal table, after winning just one gold and fourteen other medals at the [1996 Summer Olympics](/wiki/1996_Summer_Olympics "1996 Summer Olympics") in Atlanta, which led to significant changes in the management and funding of British sports and facilities.[[13]](#cite_note-14)

[London](/wiki/London "London") also won the right to host the 1944 Summer Olympics. However, the 1944 games were cancelled due to the [Second World War](/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War").

fanoutqa_003313.t: Mayor of Philadelphia :: History :: 18th century :: chunk_0001
fanoutqa_003313.x:
Mayor of Philadelphia :: History :: 18th century :: chunk_0001
The first [mayor](/wiki/Mayor "Mayor") of [Philadelphia](/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia") was [Humphrey Morrey](/wiki/Humphrey_Morrey "Humphrey Morrey"), who was appointed to the position by [William Penn](/wiki/William_Penn "William Penn"), the founder of the city and the colonial-era [Province of Pennsylvania](/wiki/Province_of_Pennsylvania "Province of Pennsylvania"), which became the state of Pennsylvania following the [American Revolutionary War](/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War"). Penn subsequently appointed [Edward Shippen](/wiki/Edward_Shippen "Edward Shippen") under the city charter of 1701. The [Philadelphia City Council](/wiki/Philadelphia_City_Council "Philadelphia City Council") then elected Shippen to a second term. Subsequent mayors, who held office for one year, were elected by the Philadelphia City Council. The initial mayors of Philadelphia were not compensated and candidates sometimes objected strongly to being selected to the position, sometimes choosing even to pay a fine rather than serve in the position.

In 1704, [alderman](/wiki/Alderman "Alderman") [Griffith Jones](/wiki/Griffith_Jones_(mayor) "Griffith Jones (mayor)") was elected but declined to serve, for which he was fined twenty pounds. In 1706, [Thomas Story](/wiki/Thomas_Story "Thomas Story"), also an alderman, was similarly fined for refusing office.

In 1745, Abraham Taylor, a Philadelphia alderman, was fined thirty pounds for refusing to assume the office. The city council then elected [Joseph Turner](/wiki/Joseph_Turner_(loyalist) "Joseph Turner (loyalist)"), who also refused and was likewise fined.[[2]](#cite_note-History-2) Others who refused election included [Richard Hill](/wiki/Richard_Hill_(Pennsylvania_politician) "Richard Hill (Pennsylvania politician)") (1717), [Issac Norris](/wiki/Isaac_Norris_(mayor) "Isaac Norris (mayor)") (1722), John Mifflin, and Alexander Stedman. The press release from the [Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences](/wiki/Royal_Swedish_Academy_of_Sciences "Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences") noted: "Their experimental research methods now entirely dominate [development economics](/wiki/Development_economics "Development economics")."[[40]](#cite_note-40)[[41]](#cite_note-guardianlive-41)

The Nobel committee commented:

:   :   "Banerjee, Duflo and their co-authors concluded that students appeared to learn nothing from additional days at school. Neither did spending on textbooks seem to boost learning, even though the schools in [Kenya](/wiki/Kenya "Kenya") lacked many essential inputs. Moreover, in the Indian context Banerjee and Duflo intended to study, many children appeared to learn little: in results from field tests in the city of [Vadodara](/wiki/Vadodara "Vadodara") fewer than one in five third-grade students could correctly answer first-grade curriculum math test questions.[[41]](#cite_note-guardianlive-41)

:   :   "In response to such findings, Banerjee, Duflo and co-authors argued that efforts to get more children into school must be complemented by reforms to improve school quality."[[41]](#cite_note-guardianlive-41)

The Nobel Prize was a major recognition for their chosen field - Development Economics, and for the use of Randomised Controlled Trials. fanoutqa_037617.x:
John Sharp (Texas politician) :: Education and early life :: chunk_0001
The son of an oil field worker and a school teacher, Sharp grew up in the small farming community of [Placedo, Texas](/wiki/Placedo,_Texas "Placedo, Texas"). In 1972, Sharp earned a [Bachelor of Arts](/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") degree in [political science](/wiki/Political_science "Political science") from [Texas A&M University](/wiki/Texas_A%26M_University "Texas A&M University") in [College Station](/wiki/College_Station,_Texas "College Station, Texas"), where he was a member of Squadron 6 in the [Corps of Cadets](/wiki/Texas_A%26M_University_Corps_of_Cadets "Texas A&M University Corps of Cadets") and was elected
[class president](/wiki/Class_president "Class president") his sophomore year, and eventually [Student Body President](/wiki/Student_government_president "Student government president").[[1]](#cite_note-:1-1) Upon graduation, he was commissioned as a [second lieutenant](/wiki/Second_lieutenant "Second lieutenant") in the [United States Army Reserves](/wiki/United_States_Army_Reserves "United States Army Reserves"). He belongs to [American Legion](/wiki/American_Legion "American Legion")[[2]](#cite_note-TXDirectory-2) Post 76 in Austin.

In 1976, Sharp received a master's degree in Public Administration from [Texas State University](/wiki/Texas_State_University "Texas State University") in [San Marcos](/wiki/San_Marcos,_Texas "San Marcos, Texas") while working full-time in Austin with the Legislative Budget Board.[[3]](#cite_note-3) In 1978, Sharp returned to [Victoria](/wiki/Victoria,_Texas "Victoria, Texas"), Texas, where he opened a real estate firm[[1]](#cite_note-:1-1) with a partner, the former County Commissioner Gene Martin.

Michael Phelps :: Swimming career :: 2008 Summer Olympics :: Beijing :: chunk_0021
Phelps set an [Olympic record](/wiki/Olympic_record "Olympic record") in the preliminary heats of the 400-meter individual medley.[[138]](#cite_note-138)[[139]](#cite_note-139) He followed that up in the final by winning the gold medal, as well as breaking his previous world record by nearly two seconds.[[140]](#cite_note-140)[[141]](#cite_note-141) This swim went on to become the longest men's world record to stand in long course meters, beating Germany's Otto Farr who held the 100 backstroke world record from 1912 until 1926.[[142]](#cite_note-142)

Phelps swam the first leg of the 4×100-meter freestyle relay in a time of 47.51 seconds (an American record for the 100-meter freestyle), and won his second gold medal of the 2008 Olympics, as well as setting his second world record of the Olympics (3:08.24).[[143]](#cite_note-143) Teammate Jason Lezak, after beginning the anchor leg more than half a body length behind [Alain Bernard](/wiki/Alain_Bernard "Alain Bernard"), managed to finish ahead of the favored French swimmer by eight hundredths of a second. The top five teams in the final finished ahead of the world record of 3:12.23 set the previous day by the American B team in a preliminary heat.[[144]](#cite_note-144) Phelps remarked that Bernard's pre-race comments of "smashing the Americans" had "fired me up more than anything else". *Le Nouvel Observateur* noted "Phelps taking the time to applaud and console Bernard" and wrote that this sportsmanship was "proof that the person who swims in the wake of Mark Spitz is also a great gentleman."[[145]](#cite_note-145)

For his third race, Phelps broke his previous world record in the 200-meter freestyle by nearly a second and won his third gold medal. He also set his third world record at the Olympics, 1:42.96, winning by nearly two seconds over silver medalist [Park Tae-hwan](/wiki/Park_Tae-hwan "Park Tae-hwan").[[146]](#cite_note-146)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Population_density_map_of_the_world.svg/500px-Population_density_map_of_the_world.svg.png)](/wiki/File:Population_density_map_of_the_world.svg)

Map of [countries by population density](/wiki/List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_population_density "List of countries and dependencies by population density")

The continent of [Asia](/wiki/Asia "Asia") covers 29.4% of the Earth's land area and has a population of around 4.75 billion (as of 2022),[[1]](#cite_note-UN_Population_Division-1) accounting for about 60% of the world population. The combined population of both [China](/wiki/China "China") and [India](/wiki/India "India") is estimated to be over 2.8 billion people as of 2022.
Asia's population is projected to grow to 5.25 billion by 2055, or about 54% of projected world population at that time.[[2]](#cite_note-q072-2) [Population growth](/wiki/Population_growth "Population growth") in Asia was close to 0.55% p.a. as of 2022, with highly disparate rates. Many [Western Asian](/wiki/Western_Asia "Western Asia") and [South Asian](/wiki/South_Asia "South Asia") countries have growth rates far above the world average, notably [Pakistan](/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan") at 2% p.a., and [India](/wiki/India "India") with a 0.6% increase in 2022. On the other hand, [East Asian](/wiki/East_Asia "East Asia") nations are in the middle of a demographic stagnation, with [China](/wiki/China "China") experiencing a small decrease of –0.06%, after years of rapidly slowing growth.
